request.system:
You assist an automated astronomer who infers how a body moves from angles-only sky observations (ecliptic longitude/latitude seen from an observer whose orbit is known). Jan, the fitting engine, fits candidate model families by least squares and compares them by Bayesian evidence. You see numerical summaries of the current best fit and its residuals, and you propose the next candidates to fit.

A candidate is either a registered family (by exact name) or a new central force law: the radial acceleration f(r) in AU/day^2 (negative = attractive) as an expression in r (heliocentric distance, AU), GM (the Sun's, 2.959e-4 AU^3/day^2, fixed) and parameters you declare with bounds and an initial value. Allowed in expressions: numbers, + - * / **, parentheses, exp, log, sqrt, tanh, pi, r, GM and your parameter names (lowercase, letters/digits/underscore). Prefer the simplest law that explains the residual structure; a new parameter must buy a clear improvement. Reply "stop": true when the residuals are consistent with noise or further candidates are unlikely to help.

parsed.analysis: The current best fit has not converged on a correct law. Its residual RMS is about 31,000 arcsec (around 8.6 deg). The noise sigma was fitted, so rms/sigma = 1 means nothing here. The residuals are strongly structured: mean east offsets of ±10,000–22,000 arcsec alternate in sign across time and distance bins, RMS is worst at small r (62,000 arcsec inside 6.6 AU), and the dominant periodogram peak is 379 d, close to annual (a parallax/geometry mismatch). The two half-orbit ellipse fits disagree badly (periods 4185 vs 12,880 d, apsidal shift about 100 deg/orbit), so there is strong non-Keplerian precession. In the best law the Newton scale p_s is pinned at its lower bound of 0.1. At every distance sampled, the -b/r^3 term (b ≈ 0.0045) is far larger than the Newtonian term, so the data want something close to a steep, nearly pure inverse-cube attraction. The earlier free power law settled at n = 1.93, probably a local minimum reached from a Newtonian start. Next I'll try a power law started near n = 3, the Newton+cubic law with p_s free to go far below 0.1, and an inverse-cube law with a 1/r^4 correction to capture the extra small-r structure.

proposals.rationale: The best law is effectively -b/r^3 with Newton suppressed. A power law started near n = 3 tests whether the earlier n = 1.93 fit was a local minimum, using only two parameters.
Same form as the current best fit, but the Newton scale was pinned at its lower bound of 0.1. Relaxing that bound lets the fit find its true optimum.

The largest residuals are at small r, near perihelion. A signed 1/r^4 correction to an inverse-cube core tests whether the force steepens or softens at small r beyond what a single power can describe.
